enrichment.short_title: Dyno-Rod franchisee search-and-seize and freezing order refused
key_facts: Dyno-Rod plc applied ex parte for search-and-seize and freezing orders against franchisees Debel Ltd and the Gaunts over alleged diversion of drainage work to connected companies Leat and Egress.
The application relied largely on an anonymous tip-off and circumstantial evidence of links between the franchisees and competing businesses.
Dyno-Rod had known of a possible Egress connection for about three years without acting, and there was no evidence that franchise work volumes had fallen.
Dyno-Rod indicated it would terminate the franchise and invoke wide post-termination restraints if ex parte relief were granted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Ex parte without-notice application for search-and-seize and freezing orders before issue of proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: All ex parte relief refused; the court held there was no strong prima facie case, no clear evidence of incriminating documents or risk of destruction, and the orders would cause disproportionate harm to the defendants' business.
enrichment.ratio: Search-and-seize and freezing orders are exceptional remedies requiring a strong prima facie case, serious damage, clear evidence of relevant documents, a real risk of destruction, and proportionality; weak circumstantial franchise-breach allegations based on an anonymous informant do not justify the 'nuclear' coupling of such orders.

enrichment.short_title: Channel Four Despatches broadcast: confidentiality right of reply rejected
key_facts: Tillery Valley Foods, an NHS hospital food supplier, sought to restrain a Channel Four Despatches programme based on covert filming at its Gwent factory by an undercover journalist.
The programme was expected to allege poor hygiene practices including coughing over food, eating on the production line, and elevated e-coli swab results.
Tillery could not obtain a defamation injunction because Channel Four intended to plead justification under Bonnard v Perryman.
Tillery instead argued for an informed right of reply via breach of confidence before broadcast.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Without-notice application for interim injunction restraining broadcast until disclosure of footage and testing protocol.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the court held Tillery had no real prospect of success on confidentiality and declined prior restraint.
enrichment.ratio: Covert workplace filming and employee confidentiality clauses do not necessarily create protectable confidential information where public interest favours disclosure; the law of confidence does not import a pre-publication right of reply, and a claim framed as confidentiality but aimed at protecting reputation should be treated like defamation under Bonnard v Perryman.
legal_issues: Whether covert factory footage had the quality of confidence
Whether contractual confidentiality created protectable information
Whether public interest in broadcast required an informed right of reply
Whether section 12(3) Human Rights Act 1998 permitted prior restraint

enrichment.short_title: Refugee false passport prosecution: s.31 defence and JR forum

statutes_considered.title: Convention relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: A former Yugoslav national entered the UK on a false Swedish passport after about 16 days in France and sought to travel onward to claim asylum in Canada.
The CPS prosecuted for using a false instrument under the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981 after he claimed asylum in the UK when intercepted.
He could not bring himself within the narrower statutory defence in section 31(2) because he had stopped in France without showing he could not reasonably expect Convention protection there.
He sought judicial review to stay the prosecution relying on Article 31 of the Refugee Convention as interpreted in ex parte Adimi.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review application to challenge CPS decision to prosecute a refugee using false documents, heard after committal for Crown Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the court held the defence was confined to section 31 of the 1999 Act, legitimate expectation could not expand it, and judicial review was not the appropriate forum for a pending Crown Court prosecution.
enrichment.ratio: After Parliament enacted section 31 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, refugees prosecuted for specified document offences in England and Wales must rely on that narrower statutory defence rather than the wider Article 31 protection declared in Adimi; treaties are not self-executing and a decision to prosecute pending Crown Court proceedings is generally not amenable to judicial review.
legal_issues: Whether Article 31 Refugee Convention remained directly enforceable after section 31 was enacted
Whether Adimi legitimate expectation survived the statutory defence
Whether prosecution for false passport use was an abuse of process
Whether judicial review was the proper means to raise the defence

key_facts: McAlpine sought to enforce a £45,194.54 adjudicator's award against Transco for interest on late certification of NEC compensation events on a Kent gas pipeline contract.
The dispute concerned interest under clauses 51.3 and 51.4 where McAlpine claimed automatic entitlement once compensation event costs were incurred.

enrichment.short_title: Dr Martens logo: foreign copyright assignment and comity
key_facts: Griggs Group claimed equitable ownership of the Dr Martens logo copyright after designer Evans assigned worldwide copyrights to Raben despite prior English-law contracts implying assignment to Griggs.
Peter Prescott QC had already held at trial that Raben, with notice of Griggs' prior interest, should assign copyright including foreign rights: see [2003] EWHC 2914 (Ch).
Before entry of the order Raben raised a new point that English courts could not order assignment of foreign copyrights absent a personal obligation to transfer.
The logo drawing had substantial commercial value across many jurisdictions where Griggs sold Dr Martens footwear.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further judgment (No 2) on a late jurisdictional objection after trial judgment and before formal order on foreign copyright assignments.
enrichment.outcome: Jurisdictional objection rejected; Griggs entitled to an order requiring Raben to assign foreign copyrights in the logo as well as the UK copyright.
enrichment.ratio: It is not a breach of international comity for an English court to adjudicate in personam on foreign copyright rights arising from an English-governed contract against a purchaser with notice of a prior equitable interest, where no foreign law is shown to extinguish that equity; the court may order assignment of foreign copyrights rather than requiring parallel proceedings worldwide.
legal_issues: Whether English courts may order assignment of foreign intellectual property
Whether comity prevents in personam relief over copyrights situate abroad
Whether a third party with notice holds property subject to a prior equitable interest
Whether foreign copyright systems extinguish English equitable rights

enrichment.short_title: 9/11 reinsurance slip: annual aggregate deductible construction
key_facts: Goshawk reinsurers sought summary judgment that they owed no indemnity to XL for about US$10m of Limited Inc store losses from the 11 September 2001 World Trade Center collapse.
The MAR 91 slip reinsurance covered stock losses in excess of the original US$5m annual aggregate deductible and underlying deductibles.
The underlying policy allowed the insurer to pay losses above US$1m per occurrence even before the AAD was exhausted.
Reinsurers argued cover responded only after full exhaustion of the US$5m AAD; insurers contended the slip tracked the underlying back-to-back deductible regime.

enrichment.ratio: Read as a whole against an 'all as per original' reinsurance slip, the Sum Insured clause incorporating the underlying AAD regime means reinsurers follow insurers' fortunes on stock losses once applicable original underlying deductibles—including the US$1m per-occurrence limit within clause 5A—are exceeded, not only after the entire US$5m annual aggregate is exhausted.

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates six-month limit and computer information date
key_facts: David Atkinson appealed by case stated after conviction for carrying an insecure load on 16 June 2002.
The summons showed an information date of 10 December 2002 but was printed on 20 December 2002, four days after the six-month limitation period.
Police now enter offence details on a linked computer system and 'validate' the information before a summons is printed.
There was no evidence whether post-entry amendments occurred after 10 December 2002, creating uncertainty over when the information was effectively laid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from a magistrates' court ruling refusing to stay proceedings as an abuse of process.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed and matter remitted with direction to decline jurisdiction because the prosecution could not prove the information was laid within six months.
enrichment.ratio: Where evidence shows a computer-generated information may have remained incomplete or been amended after the date printed on the summons, magistrates must resolve doubt on the effective laying date against the prosecution; uncertainty whether section 127 was satisfied goes to jurisdiction, not merely abuse of process.

Whether uncertainty over the information date deprives magistrates of jurisdiction

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor disciplinary acquittal: costs order restored
key_facts: Mr Hayes faced Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal allegations that he billed unjustified charges and misled a client, centred on a November 1998 lunch and a partner's train fare.
The tribunal dismissed all misconduct allegations, found the complainant incredible, and accepted Hayes' account that the lunch was a business meeting.
It criticised Hayes only for bill wording describing lunch costs as 'travel' and for lack of transparency, then made no order as to costs.
Hayes appealed under section 49 seeking his costs of about £100,000 from the Law Society.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 49 Solicitors Act 1974 against a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal costs refusal after full acquittal on conduct charges.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal order substituted with an order that Hayes receive his costs of and incidental to the hearing from the Law Society, plus appeal costs summarily assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a solicitor is resoundingly acquitted of serious dishonesty allegations brought by a dishonest client, minor billing transparency criticisms without causal link to the proceedings cannot justify depriving him of costs; Rule 22 does not support a no-costs order against a successful respondent whose conduct on the core issues was vindicated.
